problems.description: Measured convention score 0.66 with 13 violations (PascalCase classes, UPPER_CASE module constants, snake_case functions). However, most listed files (app.py, celery_app.py, celery_config.py) are NOT in this commit's diff, and the conftest.py violations are contradictory since the committed conftest.py is empty (blob e69de29). These appear to be pre-existing violations in the worktree, not introduced by this commit.
status field accepts any non-empty string with no validation against a whitelist, so the API contract is loose and callers can persist arbitrary statuses.
SonarQube delta shows +3 smells and +30 cognitive complexity; update_task has multi-branch validation logic that could be factored into helpers.

strengths: Idiomatic Flask app-factory pattern (create_app) with injectable database path enabling clean test isolation via tempfile DBs.
Request-scoped SQLite connections closed through teardown_appcontext; parameterized queries throughout (no SQL injection).
Comprehensive pytest suite covering success, 400 validation, and 404 not-found paths for all endpoints.
Clean snake_case naming, UPPER_CASE DATABASE constant, and no new bugs or duplication per SonarQube.
commit_reviews.summary: Clean, idiomatic greenfield Flask/SQLite implementation with strong tests and zero bugs, but the measured convention score (0.66) is dragged down by violations in files outside this commit's diff — which the tooling attributes to this commit despite the conflicting conftest.py entry.

problems.description: No tests added for register/login/require_auth; existing task-endpoint tests will now return 401 since every route became auth-required, so the suite is very likely broken. Security-critical code is untested.
JWT_SECRET falls back to hardcoded 'dev-secret-change-me'; if deployed without the env var, tokens are forgeable. Acceptable for a demo, but risky default.
require_auth injects `user` as a positional argument, coupling every route signature to the decorator's ordering; flask.g or a request attribute would avoid the signature-mutation pattern.
created_at uses deprecated datetime.utcnow() while JWT exp uses timezone-aware datetime.now(timezone.utc) — inconsistent timestamp conventions (naive vs aware) in the same module.
register/login do `data = request.get_json(silent=True) or {}` then `data.get(...)`; a JSON list body would raise AttributeError and 500 instead of a 400.

strengths: In-place SQLite migration (PRAGMA table_info + ALTER TABLE) preserves existing data across the schema change instead of breaking on startup
owner_id scoping is enforced in every task query (POST/GET/PUT), preventing cross-tenant data leakage
Proper password hashing via werkzeug generate/check_password_hash and timezone-aware JWT exp
Follows the existing create_app factory, get_db, and error-handler patterns; changed file code is snake_case/UPPER_CASE compliant
commit_reviews.summary: Well-structured feature addition that correctly layers JWT auth with per-user ownership and a data-preserving migration, but ships without tests (likely breaking the existing suite) and a risky default secret.

problems.description: send_notification_email duplicates output via both logger.info() and print() for the same message; pick one channel to avoid noisy/duplicated logs.

The bare except Exception around send_notification_email.delay() catches all failures including configuration errors, masking misconfig; acceptable for fire-and-forget but scope could be narrowed to broker/connection errors.
All tests mock send_notification_email, so the task function body itself (message formatting, return payload) has no direct coverage.

Measured: module-level constants in celery_config.py (broker_url, result_backend, task_routes, etc.) and the celery_app instance are snake_case rather than UPPER_CASE. Discrepancy flagged: lowercase keys are the idiomatic Celery config style, and several reported violations (app.py, conftest.py) are pre-existing files outside this diff.

strengths: Clean separation of concerns: Celery app, config/routing, and Flask app live in dedicated modules with clear responsibilities.
Fire-and-forget enqueue with broker-outage isolation keeps the API response path intact (verified by test_notification_broker_failure_does_not_break_response).
Comprehensive trigger tests: completion, non-completion, title-only, no-retrigger on already-completed, owner-username recipient, and failure resilience.
Env-driven broker/backend config with sensible localhost defaults; explicit JSON serialization and UTC timezone settings.
Uses task owner username as recipient, consistent with the existing JWT auth model.
commit_reviews.summary: Architecturally sound, well-tested Celery integration for async completion notifications whose low convention score is dragged by idiomatic lowercase Celery config keys and pre-existing violations outside this diff.

problems.description: Generic base CRUD interpolates column names from dict keys into SQL via f-strings; safe with internal callers but invites misuse if untrusted input ever flows through fields.
create_user/create_task perform an INSERT followed by an extra SELECT round trip via get_by_id instead of returning the row directly.
BaseRepository.update commits but returns nothing, forcing callers (update_task) to re-query the row.

strengths: Centralizes all SQLite access in a repository layer so route handlers never touch sqlite3 directly — a clean separation of persistence from request handling.
Generic BaseRepository with table-specific subclasses eliminates the duplicated SQL previously scattered across route handlers.
Preserves ownership-scoped queries (get_by_id_and_owner, list_by_owner) so the refactor doesn't weaken authorization semantics.
Commit's own code follows conventions (PascalCase classes, snake_case methods, UPPER_CASE constants); introduces zero new convention violations.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, pattern-following repository-layer refactor that removes duplicated SQL from handlers and introduces no new technical debt, though the measured 0.66 convention score reflects pre-existing violations in untouched files (app.py, celery_app.py, celery_config.py, conftest.py) rather than this commit.

problems.description: `count_by_owner` runs a full COUNT(*) on every page of every request, an O(n) scan that partially undermines the constant-time benefit of keyset cursor pagination; consider making total lazy/optional or moving it to a header.

Default `RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI` hardcodes `redis://localhost:6379/3`, adding a hard runtime Redis dependency for dev/tests; flask-limiter's in-memory storage would avoid the external service requirement while keeping Redis as an opt-in for distributed deployments.
`rate_limit_key` re-implements the JWT decode logic already present in `require_auth`, duplicating token-parsing; extracting a shared helper would keep auth handling single-sourced.
Cognitive complexity +42 (largest SonarQube delta) comes from the cursor/limit parsing branches in `list_tasks`; factoring the parsing into small helper functions would flatten the handler.

strengths: Cursor/keyset pagination with the `limit + 1` has_more trick and a docstring explaining why `id` ordering preserves newest-first — a scalable choice over offset pagination.
Pagination and rate limiting are injectable through `create_app(...)` args and env vars, preserving the existing factory pattern and keeping tests hermetic.
Per-user rate-limit keys derived from the JWT `sub` with IP fallback is auth-aware and correct.
New SQL lives in `TaskRepository` following the existing repo method shape (`list_by_owner_paginated`, `count_by_owner`), keeping persistence in the repository layer.
Input validation for cursor/limit, a 429 handler, and updated tests plus a `make_client` fixture for custom rate limits show good test coverage of the new behavior.
commit_reviews.summary: Well-structured cross-cutting session that adds keyset pagination and configurable per-user rate limiting through existing patterns with tests, though the reported convention score of 0.66 reflects pre-existing violations in untouched files (app.py, celery_app.py, celery_config.py, conftest.py), not anything this commit introduced.

compounding_issues: No migration framework from the start: S2 and S3 had to hand-roll idempotent migrations (PRAGMA table_info column checks, ALTER TABLE, and a synthetic 'legacy' user to backfill pre-existing rows) because the seed used bare CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS.

Per-call SQLite connections (a fresh get_db() connection per operation) persisted through the S4 repository refactor — repositories.py kept the same open-per-method pattern instead of introducing connection reuse or transaction management.

S3 introduced a hard runtime dependency on Redis (Celery broker) with a fixed default broker URL (redis://localhost:6379/0); the task-completion path calls .delay() unconditionally, so a broker outage would break PUT /tasks in production (only tests avoid this via injectable stubs).
Security defaults left as code: JWT_SECRET='development-secret-change-me' (S2) and the rate-limiter storage URI default (S5) were never made deployment-mandatory.
key_decisions: S2: JWT auth + per-user task ownership (owner_id scoping on every query) — set the security/isolation model every later session builds on.
S2/S3: backward-compatible idempotent data migrations with a deterministic 'legacy' user so pre-existing rows remain accessible after schema changes.
S3: Celery/Redis async completion notifications, dispatched only on a real transition into 'completed' — introduced async infra plus an external broker dependency.

S4: Repository pattern extraction (BaseRepository ABC + Task/UserRepository) that moved all SQL out of app.py while preserving the response contract and test monkeypatching — the move that de-risked S5.
S5: user-aware Redis rate limiting with in-memory fallback, and cursor-based pagination as a stable GET /tasks response contract with limit validation and total counts.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved monotonically across all five sessions. S1 polished the single-file seed with strict request validation, timezone-aware timestamps, import-time schema init, and the first 3 tests. S2 delivered the biggest jump — a complete JWT auth + ownership layer with a careful legacy-data migration (4 tests). S3 added Celery notifications cleanly without disturbing existing behavior (6 tests). S4 was the riskiest step — a full repository refactor — but it was genuinely beneficial rather than churn: app.py lost all SQL, the API contract was preserved, and tests stayed green at 6. S5 closed the arc with two cross-cutting features (rate limiting and cursor pagination) built directly on the S4 abstraction and S2 auth, expanding tests to 9 and introducing a stable paged response contract. Test coverage grew 3->4->6->6->9 with zero regressions at any commit, and the final state is a clean, well-factored multi-module codebase that still passes its suite end-to-end.
story_review.summary: A disciplined, logically-sequenced story in which each session landed cleanly on the prior commit and the S4 refactor — the highest-risk step — succeeded in setting up a clean cross-cutting S5, with only minor unaddressed debt around hand-rolled migrations, per-call DB connections, and hardcoded Redis/security defaults.
